#7773. The Best Combination Squares for Accurate Layout and Repeatable Marks

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 20, 2026 12:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

A combination square earns its keep before the first cut, helping woodworkers and DIYers mark straight crosscuts, check corners, lay out miters, and repeat measurements. We tested seven of these versatile measuring tools to find out how accurately they measured and whether their blades stayed put once locked.

A small layout error can carry through a project, leaving joints that won’t close or parts that don’t align. Our Best Overall pick, the Starrett 11H-12-4R 12-Inch Steel Combination Square, delivered accurate results in our squaring and miter checks, and its blade held its setting during our retention test. Its hardened-steel blade and fine graduations make it a strong choice for detailed layout work.

Our tested picks include compact woodworking squares for small jobs, longer models for wider workpieces, and options with useful extras. Read on for our hands-on findings and the features to consider when choosing the best combination square.

Whether you’re choosing tools for building the essential toolbox or adding a specialized square to your workshop, these tested picks cover a range of sizes, materials, and features.

The Starrett 11H-12-4R combines a 12-inch hardened-steel blade with a cast-iron head for checking square, laying out miters, and transferring measurements. Its photo-engraved 4R graduations run from eighths down to sixty-fourths of an inch, and the head includes a bubble level and scribe. A reversible lock bolt allows the blade to be secured in either orientation.

We were impressed with its accuracy in our layout tests. After scribing a fine line against a straight factory edge, we flipped the square and scribed again from the same starting point; the lines aligned. The 45-degree face also checked out when we marked opposing angles and checked that they formed a right angle. We checked the blade against a manufactured straightedge and used a light behind it to look for gaps. Its graduations also agreed with our reference steel rule.

Just as important for repeated measurements, the blade held its setting after we tightened the lock and gently tapped the tool. That secure hold means less need to stop and recheck a setting between marks. The inch-only scale is a limitation for metric work, and the cast-iron head deserves careful handling to protect its measuring faces. For users working in fractional inches, however, the Starrett delivers an accurate layout and dependable blade retention in our tests.

What our tester says: “I was really impressed by how closely the lines aligned in my flip test and how well the blade held its setting after gentle tapping. The quality of this square is obvious.” –Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Starrett combination square at Amazon or Zoro.

For small projects, a 6-inch combination square is just right. This Ace square offers a stainless steel blade, a machined cast-zinc head, and both inch and metric markings in a compact package. It’s a good option for homeowners who need to mark short crosscuts, check corners, or transfer measurements. Its size also makes it a practical choice to keep in a toolbox for quick repairs.

We put the Ace through the same accuracy checks as the larger squares, and it performed well. Its squaring and miter faces passed our opposing-line tests, and the ruler markings matched our reference steel rule. The blade also passed our straightness and light-gap checks. Once secured, it resisted movement when we gently tapped it—a useful result for anyone making several marks at the same setting.

The included screw-in scribe and bubble level add versatility without requiring separate accessories. We also like having millimeters alongside fractional inches. The main compromise is reach: the short blade won’t extend across wider stock, and its finest inch divisions are thirty-seconds. We’d consider it for small layout jobs or as a companion to a longer square.

Get the Ace combination square at Ace Hardware.

A combination square needs to hold a measurement as reliably as it establishes one, and the Mr. Pen delivered on that requirement in our tests. We tightened its spring-loaded brass bolt, gently tapped the tool, and checked the setting again. The blade hadn’t crept, giving us confidence in its ability to maintain an offset for repeated marking. Its 12-inch stainless steel blade provides useful reach for general woodworking layout, while the included brass scribe and bubble level round out the basic features.

Accuracy was also good across our checks. The ruler agreed with our reference steel rule, and we found no issues when checking blade straightness against a manufactured edge and looking for gaps against a flat surface. Both angle faces performed well, too: the reversed square produced matching scribed lines, and opposing marks from the 45-degree face formed a right angle. These results support using it for everyday tasks such as marking crosscuts, checking assembled corners, and laying out miters.

The blade carries inch and centimeter scales, with fractional-inch divisions in eighths, sixteenths, and thirty-seconds. That selection covers many common layout measurements, although users who work in sixty-fourths will need a finer rule. We’d consider the Mr. Pen for a general-purpose woodworking kit, particularly when secure blade retention and a full-length rule matter more than extra-fine graduations.

Get the Mr. Pen combination square at Amazon or Mr. Pen.

The Milwaukee MLSQC12 adds a magnetic head to the familiar sliding-square design, giving it applications beyond wood layout. Two rare-earth magnets are designed to hold against steel and other ferrous materials, making the square an option for users who also work with conduit or metal stock. Its larger head provides more contact with the workpiece, while machined 45- and 90-degree faces handle squaring and miter layout.

We checked those working faces rather than assuming the additional features meant better accuracy. The Milwaukee passed both flip tests, producing aligned square lines and opposing 45-degree marks that formed a true right angle. Its 12-inch blade also checked straight, and the graduations agreed with our reference steel rule. We paid particular attention to blade retention: after setting and tightening the draw bolt, we gently tapped the square and found that the measurement held. That matters when transferring the same dimension to multiple pieces.

Other features include a precision-etched stainless steel blade, a Sharpsite bubble vial, and a scribe pin stored in the head. A scribe hole at the 1-inch mark provides another layout option. The magnetic feature has an obvious material limitation—it won’t hold to wood, aluminum, or other nonferrous surfaces—but the square remains usable conventionally on those materials. We’d consider this model for a workshop that handles both woodworking and steel layout.

Get the Milwaukee combination square at The Home Depot, Acme Tools, or Zoro.

The Irwin 6-inch metal combination square comes with a cast-zinc head, a stainless steel blade, and black precision-etched scales. That construction gives it the familiar features of a larger workshop square in a shorter format. We’d reach for this square when laying out small parts or checking narrow stock, where a longer blade can extend unnecessarily beyond the workpiece.

In testing, the Irwin handled the essentials well. We verified the ruler against our reference steel rule and checked the blade for straightness and gaps against a flat surface. It passed those checks, along with our tests of the square and miter faces. We also found that tightening the blade lock kept the setting from shifting even after gentle tapping. For repeated measurements, that secure adjustment is every bit as important as having an accurate scale.

The main limitation is the blade’s reach. Six inches is useful for close layout work, but it won’t span the same material widths as a 12-inch square. We’d keep the Irwin available for smaller measurements and corner checks, then use a longer model when the job calls for extending a line farther across a board.

Get the Irwin combination square at Amazon and Acme Tools.

WorkPro pairs two useful layout tools in this combination square set: a 7-inch rafter square for angle marking and a 12-inch combination square for adjustable measurements. The tools serve complementary purposes. The rafter square’s lipped fence registers against a board’s edge, while the combination square’s sliding head lets users establish depths and offsets. For someone assembling a woodworking tool kit, having both expands the range of layout jobs the set can handle.

We concentrated our accuracy testing on the combination square, which has a die-cast zinc-alloy head and a matte stainless steel blade. Its ruler matched our reference steel rule, and the blade passed our straightness and light-gap checks. The 90- and 45-degree faces also produced the expected results in our flip tests. After tightening the adjustment screw, we gently tapped the tool and checked for blade movement; the setting remained unchanged.

The combination square includes a metal scribe and bubble level, plus scales with sixteenth-inch, thirty-second-inch, and millimeter divisions. Users needing sixty-fourth-inch measurements will want a finer rule. The separate aluminum rafter square adds a fixed layout tool that can also serve as a crosscut guide. We’d consider this set for general carpentry projects that call for both adjustable measurements and quick angle layout.

What our tester says: “I like having a rafter square and an adjustable combination square together for framing layout tasks. The WorkPro square passed all accuracy checks and held its setting securely.” –Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the WorkPro combination square set at Amazon or WorkPro.

When a standard 12-inch square won’t reach far enough across a workpiece, the iGaging’s 24-inch blade provides another foot of working length. That extra reach makes it worth considering for wider boards, shelving, and furniture components. We’d choose this size for projects where extending a layout line farther from an edge is necessary.

A longer blade makes straightness particularly important, so we checked the iGaging against a manufactured straightedge and looked for light gaps against a flat surface. It performed well in both checks, and its ruler markings agreed with our reference steel rule. The angle tests were also spot-on: reversing the square produced aligned scribed lines, while opposing marks from the miter face formed a right angle. We also checked whether the blade would creep after tightening the lock and gently tapping the tool. It retained its setting, supporting consistent measurements between marks.

The trade-off is handling and storage. A 2-foot blade needs more clearance around the workpiece and more room in a drawer or tool cabinet. For small parts or crowded work areas, we’d keep a shorter square nearby. The iGaging makes the most sense as a dedicated tool for larger layout jobs.

Get the iGaging combination square at Amazon.

We tested seven combination squares, evaluating ease of use, accuracy, readability, durability, and value. To check each square’s 90-degree face, we registered its head against a straight factory edge, scribed a fine line, then flipped the square and scribed again from the same point, checking for divergence. We tested the 45-degree faces by marking opposing angles and checking whether they formed a true 90-degree angle.

We compared blade straightness against a manufactured straightedge and held each blade against a flat surface with light behind it to reveal gaps. We also checked ruler graduations against a trusted steel rule. To test blade retention, we tightened each lock, gently tapped the tool, and rechecked its setting. These checks informed our accuracy assessments; we also considered adjustment, scale legibility, construction, included features, and price when evaluating the squares.

A combination square pairs a sliding ruler with a head for checking 90- and 45-degree angles, measuring depths, and marking consistent offsets. Understanding squares, levels, and plumbs can help you compare different types of squares and their applications. Compact models suit small parts, while longer blades extend across wider workpieces. Some sets add center-finding or protractor heads, and magnetic models provide holding assistance on steel.

Blade length determines how far a combination square can measure or mark from an edge. A 6-inch model suits small parts, narrow stock, and confined spaces. A 12 inch combination square offers a practical balance of reach and handling for general woodworking, while 18- and 24-inch blades accommodate wider boards and larger components.

A combination square’s usefulness depends on the relationship between its blade and head. The blade should be straight, the graduations correctly spaced, and the working faces accurately set at 90 and 45 degrees. Fine scale divisions alone don’t establish accuracy; a detailed ruler cannot compensate for an out-of-square head.

Check a new square before relying on it. Register the head against a known straight edge, draw a fine line, then flip the square and draw again from the same point. Diverging lines indicate a problem. Keep contact surfaces free of debris, and repeat the check after a drop or impact that could affect alignment.

Look for a blade with crisp, easy-to-read markings in the units and increments you use most. For standard woodworking, 1/16-inch graduations are often used for general layouts, while 1/32-inch divisions are crucial for making tight fits in trim and moldings. If you’re more familiar with metrics, you’ll want to choose millimeter markings.

Squares with etched markings tend to be more expensive, but they also hold up better than printed markings that can wear off with repeated handling. Dark markings on satin-finished blades can be easier to read under bright shop lights.

For reliable combination square use, the blade should slide smoothly when the lock is loosened and remain fixed when tightened. Binding makes small adjustments frustrating, while excessive play can prevent the blade from seating consistently. Check that the head sits firmly against the workpiece without rocking and that the adjustment knob is easy to grip.

Check a new square before relying on it. Register the head against a known straight edge, draw a fine line, then flip the square and draw again from the same point. Diverging lines indicate a problem. Keep contact surfaces free of debris, and repeat the check after a drop or impact that could affect alignment.

These answers explain how to use a combination square, check its accuracy, and keep it working properly.

A combination square is a measuring and layout tool with a ruler that slides through an adjustable head. The standard head provides 90- and 45-degree working faces, allowing the tool to check corners, mark miters, and measure depths or offsets.

Rest the head firmly against a workpiece’s edge to mark or check 90- and 45-degree angles. Slide and lock the blade to measure depths, check heights, or mark consistent offsets. The removable blade also serves as a ruler. If included, the bubble vial checks level, and the scribe scratches fine layout lines.For checking level over longer distances, use a dedicated level suited to the job. Our guide to the different types of levels explains the options and their applications.

Accuracy varies by model and manufacturing tolerances. A straight blade, accurately machined head, and secure lock all contribute to reliable results. Fine graduations don’t guarantee accuracy, and price alone doesn’t establish it. Check any new square before use and recheck it after a drop or impact.

Use a board with a known straight edge. Hold the square’s head firmly against that edge and draw a fine line along the blade. Flip the square, register the head against the same edge, and align the blade with the line’s starting point. Draw again. The lines should coincide; any divergence indicates a squareness error, assuming the board’s edge is straight and the tool is seated correctly.

To set the blade, loosen the locking knob, slide it to the desired measurement, and retighten. If the square appears inaccurate, remove the blade, clean its groove and the head’s contact surfaces, then reassemble and repeat the accuracy check.Calibration procedures vary by design. Some squares permit correction at the blade’s seating surfaces, but filing or sanding removes material permanently and can worsen the error. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions or seek service or replacement if cleaning doesn’t resolve the problem.

Wipe away dust, moisture, and debris after use, paying particular attention to the blade groove and locking mechanism. Dry the tool before storing it, and apply any lubricant or rust protection according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Avoid abrasives on the graduations and measuring faces. Store the square where its blade won’t bend, and protect the head from drops and impacts.

Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual)

#7770. This is the Right Height for Mounting a TV on the Wall

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Manasa Reddigari, Theresa Clement, Phillip Tinner

Updated Nov 20, 2026 2:12 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

How high you should mount a TV on the wall is a question that stumps binge-watchers and cinephiles alike. Position the TV too high or low, and you’ll have to crane your neck or slump your shoulders to take in the on-screen action. A misplaced TV can also be a pain to remove and reinstall at another height, which is why it’s in your best interest to get it right the first time.

Manufacturers and home entertainment enthusiasts recommend mounting a TV at eye level for optimal viewing, but the best TV height for you also depends on TV wall mount type, screen size, and other factors. The answer to how high should a TV be mounted sometimes varies slightly for those reasons, but these rules of thumb will help you come to the right decision.

As you think about how high to mount a TV, most experts use the center of the TV screen as the main point of reference, no matter the screen size. Unless you’re mounting a TV for just one person to use, keeping the center of the TV at a comfortable viewing height for most people should be the goal. Forty-two inches from the floor to the center of the screen is the ideal TV mount height under most circumstances.

For tailored comfort, however, you can actually factor your height, and the height of fellow household members, into your TV’s height from the floor. You’ll find a more exact center point for your TV mount by measuring the distance from the floor to each household member’s eye level when sitting. Add those measurements together and divide by the total number of people for your bespoke TV wall mount height.

Note that while TV size doesn’t always affect mounting height, a TV’s dimensions matter when considering optimal viewing distance. If you have a large, 65-inch or 75-inch TV, it may be uncomfortable to watch if your seating is too close to the wall it’s mounted on, regardless of how high or low it’s mounted. In these and similar cases, use a TV mount height calculator to simplify the math and guesswork involved in determining the best TV viewing distance and height for your space.

These LED strip lights connect to your TV’s USB port to light up your screen from behind. See our full review.

Not all of the seats in a living room are going to be the same height. An open floor plan with counter-height bar stools, bar-height stools, and a sofa, for example, can complicate TV mounting height. Counter-height bar stools are higher off of the floor than sofa seats—anywhere from 24 to 29 inches to reach the counter. Bar-height stools are even taller, at 29 to 33 inches.

If the seats in a room are at various heights, or the room in question isn’t a living room, consider the following approaches.

There are several other spatial and functional considerations to account for when determining the position and height of a wall-mounted TV. In your home, these may include:

When thinking about how high to hang a TV, you shouldn’t position it so high that viewers need to tilt their heads up more than 35 degrees from eye level in order to see the top of the screen, according to the Society of Motion Picture & Television Engineers.

Tilting a TV’s screen downward is one way to position it higher than eye level without causing discomfort or neck strain, if necessary. This requires upgrading from a basic low-profile mount (which is stationary) to one of two other types of TV mounts: a tilting wall mount (which can move up or down) or full-motion mount (which can swivel in all directions). For a full walkthrough of how to install either type of mount, check out our guide on how to mount a TV to the wall.

Deciding where to mount a TV on the wall can be confusing. Televisions are heavy and expensive items, so it’s important to get it right on the first try. Knowing how high to mount your TV depends on a few factors, and keeping the center of the screen at eye level is the most critical. While professional TV mount installation is always an option, careful measurements and the above tips will get your TV properly positioned for a comfortable premiere.

#7769. Autumn in a Montana Garden

Hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

My detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

The back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

An ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

Thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!

By Gretchen Heber, Bob Vila, Manasa Reddigari

Given a kitchen’s function as a social space, transit zone, food prep and cooking hub, and display area for decor, it’s probably one of the trickier rooms to light properly. Proper illumination also makes it easier to stow or retrieve items in and under cabinets high or low, allows you to slice and dice with greater safety and precision, and can even make a kitchen look and feel larger.

While many homeowners cite a lack of natural light as the reason their kitchens are dim, artificial lighting of the wrong type or in the wrong location can make the problem worse. When you’re revamping your kitchen lighting design, it’s smart to assess everything from function and fixture to the type of light bulbs you use. Ahead, find solutions to common kitchen lighting challenges to ensure the best kitchen lighting for all your needs.

A solid kitchen lighting strategy should ideally have fixtures in all of the following categories:

A layered approach helps minimize shadows, which often result from the exclusive use of overhead lighting, and glare, which can stem from only using bright task lighting.

The VyanLight Motion-Sensor LED Lights are easy to install and ideal for brightening dark areas. See our full review.

Look for the best fixtures in each of the three lighting categories:

Certain LED light fixtures, such as LED strips, cast a beam of light onto a surface that is brightest and most concentrated at the center of the beam and less bright on the edges. This is suitable for countertops made of butcher block, stone, or another material with a flat or matte finish. But with marble, granite, or similarly glossy materials, the center of the beam can produce a distracting glare even when placed a few feet away from it. To avoid this, place LED light strips inside light housings, which are aluminum channels with frosted covers that help diffuse bright light and minimize glare on shiny kitchen surfaces.

Incandescent, compact fluorescent light (CFL), and LED light bulbs for the kitchen come in one of three color temperatures that describe the color characteristics of the light the bulb emits. There’s Soft White (2700K to 3000 Kelvins (K)), Cool White/Bright White (3500K to 4100K), and Daylight (5000K to 6500K). The higher the bulb temperature, the cooler (i.e., bluer) the light it emits; the lower the temperature, the warmer (i.e., more amber) the light. Choose the color temperature best suited for the function of the fixture:

Remodeling your kitchen to include a natural ambient light source such as a skylight or one or more windows can lend extra warmth to the room and fill any gaps in the light coverage of your artificial light fixtures. Even in a packed kitchen, there will often be vacant spots where you can install a window, including:

Providing effective and attractive kitchen lighting is simply a matter of layering appropriate lighting types into your kitchen lighting design. Plan out and install the right mix of ambient, task, and accent lighting and your space will be well-lit and safe. With the right kitchen ceiling lights, your beautiful new space will be ready for festive gatherings with family and friends.

For safety and functionality, you’ll want lights that provide ambient and task light. Depending on your setup, you may also need accent lighting to highlight special features in your space. Be sure to find lights that are properly rated for the wet, potentially grimy environment of a kitchen.

First determine the functionality of the lighting you need. Then consider the decor of your home and which style of light fixture is the best match. Pricing, too, may be a factor, as there is a wide range of prices associated with lighting and you’ll want to select kitchen light fixtures that align with your budget.

Choose a fixture that emits adequate lighting for your environment, and select one that complements your design style.  You’ll likely have to peruse lots of web stores to find the kitchen chandelier that’s just perfect for your space, but the effort is worth it.

#7760. How to Use a Portable Gas Generator the Right Way

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Katelin Hill, Glenda Taylor, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 20, 2026 4:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

During a power outage, a generator that runs on gasoline can provide enough juice to keep your lights on, your groceries from spoiling, and your fans spinning. Set up a portable unit outside your home, and connect appliances inside to its numerous outlets via extension cords. Exactly how many appliances it’ll power at once depends on the wattage that generator can handle.

While a portable generator might cost several hundred or even thousands of dollars depending on size and model, when compared to a standby generator, which would kick on automatically to power your home, it’s certainly less expensive. Plus, you may not need a professional electrician to install a portable generator, and you can easily take the unit with you should you move. All that said, proper operation of the machine is crucial to ensure the safety of your family and your community.

Before you start up a portable generator, bear in mind these two essential considerations:

WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

Before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

Next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

Before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

Follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

Use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

To shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

Wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

When running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

#7757. The Science Behind Healthy Indoor Air (and How to Achieve It in Your Home)

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 20, 2026 5:07 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Maintaining healthy indoor air quality is essential for protecting members of your household from hidden carcinogens, allergens, and harmful particulates. Pollutants can enter your living space from a range of sources, including building materials that emit volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and poor ventilation that traps moisture and encourages mold growth.

While clues like window condensation, musty odors, or unexplained respiratory symptoms can signal trouble, invisible, odorless threats such as radon and carbon monoxide often go undetected without the right equipment. We spoke to indoor air quality experts to identify the top five indoor air pollutants in U.S. homes and how to fix or mitigate them.

This monitor impressed our product testers with accurate readings, and it connects to an app where users can find air quality reports for their home.

Particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, says Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when new furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” says Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” says Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”

Biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, says Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent issue and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

Quiet, effective and easy to use, this commercial-grade unit cleans the air with a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter.

Everyday activities such as cooking and showering introduce moisture into the home. “When excess moisture is not adequately removed, particularly in bathrooms, basements, and other low-ventilation areas, conditions can become more favorable for mold and mildew growth,” notes Meyers. You might notice foggy mirrors that take a long time to clear, condensation on windows, musty odors, bathrooms that remain damp long after use, and visible mold or mildew.

#7752. You Can Now Get a Battery Just for Your Fridge—But Is It Better Than a Generator?

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 20, 2026 7:34 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

Backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

Just in 2026, this new style hard-launched with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

Fridge-optimized batteries all share three main hallmarks:

Think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most important kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an important appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

Kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” says Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.)

Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

“It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” says Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”

The design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”

“When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen says. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really important element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”

It’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app shows outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

“[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”

There’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel says. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”

A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

Using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these new backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

“Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most important appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan says. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”

If your utility company offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing plan, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

For the average homeowner, the main way to save on these plans is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, users specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

Especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

Bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

The mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

On paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most important household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

One distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too quickly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”

From the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

Given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

BioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

#7750. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

#7744. "Can AI Ace Your Exam? A Penn Law Experiment," by Prof. R. Polk Wagner

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"On two exams, both scored on an open, non-saturated scale, it outscored every enrolled student."

A very interesting preprint; here's the Abstract:

I report a controlled experiment that ran a frontier large language model through eleven real University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School final exams in Spring 2026 and sent the machine's answers out for blind grading alongside the work of enrolled students. Each exam was answered twice: once with no course materials in the model's context (the "no-materials" arm, relying on the model's training alone) and once with the course syllabus and an outline supplied (the "with-materials" arm). Three findings emerge.

First, the model is broadly competitive: across the ten exams returned with grades, it passed every one, sat at or above the class median on every one, and reached the top decile on seven. On two exams, both scored on an open, non-saturated scale, it outscored every enrolled student.

Second, the benefit of supplying course materials is real but concentrated and uneven. It is large on multiple-choice components, small to absent on essays, and on one exam the materials helped the machine's multiple-choice score while hurting its essay—so the gain vanishes when the two are averaged into a single number. The subject of the exam matters as much as its format.

Third, faculty graders detected the AI submissions at a high rate, but mostly through signals that are easy to remove: formatting artifacts, identification-number placement, even a reversed quotation-mark glyph. The detection that survives those fixes is content-based—two independently generated answers that read as though written by the same hand, and a voice that does not match time-pressured student work. One grader was confident enough in detection to decline to grade the AI answers at all.

I read these results less as a verdict than as a measurement problem: when a model that never took the course can top the curve, it is no longer clear that the time-limited, high-stakes final is measuring what we have long assumed it measures—mastery of this course—rather than fluency in a genre the machine commands. That genre was always a contrivance built for grading, not a faithful model of practice, so the machine's success says less about lawyering than the headline suggests; but it says a good deal about how much weight the instrument can still bear.

The urgent ask the experiment surfaces is intentionality: that faculty be clear about what each assessment is meant to measure, and recognize that AI is widening an already-real gap between the law-school exam and the practice it stands in for. The responses will range—from rethinking assessment top to bottom, to narrower adjustments, to simply naming the mismatch and grading with it in view—and reasonable colleagues will differ

Like a rain jacket for your hands, waterproof gloves are essential gear for those working—or playing—outdoors in cold or inclement weather. For outdoor sports enthusiasts, they keep hands dry and protect against frostbite. For those who work outdoors, they are essential because they offer protection from grease, mud, and other wet messes.

We searched out a diverse collection of waterproof gloves for a wide variety of tasks in all seasons. Then we tested their ability to keep hands dry and comfortable in tough conditions. The Carhartt Waterproof Insulated Gloves earned our pick as the best waterproof gloves for men for their reliable waterproofing, comfortable insulation, and affordable price, and the MCTi Ski Gloves for Women topped our women’s picks for their watertight protection, flexible fit, and responsive touch-screen fingertips.

Bottom line: Discover the best waterproof gloves of 2026, tested for durability, comfort, and specific needs, ensuring dry and warm hands in any condition.

We initially selected the following gloves based on the quality of their construction, their durability, and the other features outlined previously. Then we tested them to discover how they held up under wet, slippery conditions. Find out how they performed in the reviews ahead.

Men looking for a long-lasting pair of gloves to keep their hands dry and warm may find what they’re looking for in Carhartt’s waterproof insulated gloves. From the shell to the liner to the palm pad, these gloves are made of 100 percent polyester. They provide a warm, durable, and waterproof barrier between the skin and the elements.

A liner made with Carhartt’s FastDry moisture-wicking technology prevents sweat from collecting inside the gloves, and a waterproof insert provides an extra layer of protection from the elements. Adjustable hook-and-loop closures and elastic cuffs keep hands snug while keeping out cold air and elements.

In our tests, these Carhartt waterproof work gloves were as comfortable as they were waterproof. They performed perfectly on all three of our waterproof tests. They stayed dry under the shower and when immersed in water while providing excellent holding ability thanks to the textured grip area. Three-dimensional construction lets the hand rest in a natural position and delivers good dexterity for gripping and holding. Although we didn’t test specifically for winter warmth, these gloves are deeply insulated for cold-weather work. However, the bulky profile takes away the ability to pick up small or thin items from a flat surface or to reach into a pants pocket.

What our tester says: “These got ‘Best Overall’ because they’re not only toasty and affordable, but they also make an excellent choice for winter chores while not looking like work gloves.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Carhartt waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Women on the hunt for warm, waterproof gloves may want to look at MCTi’s ski gloves. They pair a polyurethane outer shell with a faux leather palm and thumb-grip area for holding ski poles or other slippery objects. On the gloves’ interior, a waterproof liner helps keep moisture from reaching the skin.

MCTi’s gloves also contain 120 grams of Thinsulate insulation that keeps hands warm in temperatures as cold as -10 degrees Fahrenheit without adding much bulk. Handy elastic wrist leashes make keeping track of the gloves easier if the wearer removes them, and sensitive touch-screen pads on three fingers allow the wearer to answer a phone or send a text without having to take off the gloves.

In our tests, these ski gloves by MCTi seemed more like general-use winter gloves. The waterproof feature is on point, with zero water intrusion during testing and a capable grip in wet conditions. Not only that, but the insulation was less puffy than some of the other gloves we tested, which improved dexterity and flexibility for gripping and handling small items. The touch-screen fingertips worked well. Moreover, they’re available in an assortment of accent colors: gray, red, white, rose, and yellow.

Get the MCTi waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Men looking for lightweight protection from the weather may want to consider Ozero’s men’s thermal gloves, which provide warmth and weather resistance without a lot of bulk. These gloves feature a water-resistant and windproof polyester construction that keeps the wearer’s hands dry and warm in inclement weather (most of the shell fabric is indeed waterproof, but the seams and touch-screen pads on two fingers are not, hence the “water-resistant” designation). This pair is a good choice for cycling, running, walking, or other outdoor pursuits.

These gloves may not be well suited to subzero temperatures, but they’re suitable for regular winter wear and have some nice features. The gloves’ thumbs and index fingers contain sensors that are touch-screen compatible, and the palms are covered in grippy silica gel pods to help users maintain a good grip on phones and other belongings. Elastic cuffs keep out the elements. These gloves fit snugly; the manufacturer suggests sizing up for a more relaxed fit.

These mid-weight lifestyle gloves are built for everyday travel and tasks in frosty weather, but not in pouring rain. Our rain simulation and immersion tests revealed numerous water entry points. Water resistance was good in our aggressive rain simulation for about a minute before leaks developed, so we believe the gloves could keep hands mostly or completely dry during an average rainstorm. They provided excellent grip for wet items. The touch-screen feature worked well, and the snug, low-profile fit allowed us to pick up a key that was lying flat on a countertop. Also note that these gloves cost less than most of the others we tested. Moreover, they are slim and flexible and easily fit into jacket pockets.

Get the Ozero waterproof gloves at Amazon or Walmart.

Leather work gloves are a necessity when working near hot surfaces and sparks in addition to protecting the hands from abrasion, cuts, and punctures. Youngstown Glove Company’s FR Waterproof Leather Utility gloves incorporate both leather and Kevlar, a synthetic fabric commonly used for protection, along with a waterproof, windproof, breathable polyurethane barrier. These gloves, which have earned American National Standards Institute (ANSI) compliance for welding, provide Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)-approved protection for a wide range of tasks. However, they don’t provide adequate protection for electrical work.

Youngstown’s waterproof utility work gloves delivered good waterproof and wet-grip performances in our three wet tests. Although we got the leather so thoroughly wet that the gloves became heavy, the waterproof barrier prevented water intrusion to the skin. Wet grip was not a problem. We were pleasantly surprised by the dexterity that these bulky gloves provided, thanks to their three-dimensional construction and a naturally relaxed hand posture. Overall, we would not recommend these gloves for extended use in a watery environment because those conditions would cause the leather to degrade quickly. However, those who need a sturdy and comfortable insulated glove for working in the elements may want to look at these.

Get the Youngstown waterproof gloves at Amazon, JB Tools, or Youngstown Glove Company.

Carhartt’s Cold Snap insulated work gloves offer both cold-weather protection and long-lasting construction that’s tough enough for the jobsite. With warm insulation on the outer shell and a reinforced palm, these polyester gloves are reinforced with leather for extra durability. They’re waterproof and have a nose wipe on the thumb, making them a good choice for working in rough weather.

Cold Snap gloves feature some of Carhartt’s proprietary materials, including a FastDry lining for wicking moisture and Storm Defender waterproofing treatment. They have a thick cuff with an adjustable drawstring for improved weather protection. A small section of goatskin around the finger and thumb area provides added grip.

Our second pair of Carhartt waterproof work gloves performed nearly as well as the first. It provided excellent waterproof and wet-grip performance along with excellent dexterity, considering the lofty insulation. The polyester and leather exterior sheds water very well instead of becoming saturated and heavy. We liked the drawcord cuff on these gloves a little less than we liked the hook-and-loop strap closure on our “Best Overall” selection because the barrel-cord tightener is harder to manipulate with gloved hands. Nevertheless, pairing outstanding waterproofing, warmth, and comfort with a great look is the winning recipe for an all-around great pair of gloves.

Get the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves on Amazon.

No more freezing hands when you try to take a pic or return an important text. These low-profile knitted Sealskinz gloves offer triple-layer insulated waterproof, windproof protection from the elements with touch-screen-capable fingertips and outstanding range of motion. The nylon and elastane outer layer offers excellent durability with silicone-printed grips on the palm and fingers for a secure grip. A mid-layer windproof, waterproof, breathable membrane keeps the warmth in and the elements out. The lining is made of merino wool, nylon, and elastane for added warmth and breathability.

These Sealskinz gloves offered a lot of things we really liked but a few things we didn’t. We appreciated that they were truly 100 percent waterproof, both in our simulated rain test and when immersed in water. They also offer outstanding wet-grip capability, with touch-perfect touch-screen functionality. The low-profile design, moderate amount of insulation, and superior wet performance are perfect for getting outside on those miserable raw days when it’s 30 degrees Fahrenheit with freezing rain. But we didn’t love the semi-absorbent exterior because it holds on to more than its share of water, even though the water never reached our hands. It makes these otherwise excellent gloves feel heavy and a little bit squelchy. However, these may be the best gloves when wet weather threatens.

Get the Sealskinz waterproof gloves at Amazon or Sealskinz.

Hestra’s Army Leather Heli Ski 3-Finger Gloves are designed for men and women who spend their time atop some of the coldest mountains. These three-finger gloves are constructed from Hestra’s windproof, breathable, and water-resistant Triton fabric, with goat leather on the palms and fingers for improved grip in cold and slippery conditions.

The insides of these Hestra gloves are made of a very thin polyester fiber with efficient insulating properties, which makes them warm without being overly bulky. The oversize cuffs feature a drawstring closure to keep out snow and moisture, and leashes ensure the gloves won’t get lost. These Army Leather Heli gloves are available in three colors.

These gloves looked great and performed better than expected in our tests, but they were not totally waterproof. We anticipated soaking-wet hands because of the leather and “water- resistant” fabric. In our tests, the leather eventually became wet, and some moisture from outside did seep inside. They offered an OK but not great grip when wet. The best advantages of these gloves are the finger configuration, which offers better warmth than a conventional glove and better articulation than a mitten. That said, we did not test for performance in cold weather. On the downside, the leather must be regularly oiled (a tube is included), and they take a long time to dry once wet.

Get the Hestra Heli waterproof gloves at Amazon, REI, or Backcountry.com.

Built in the style of traditional cuff-length work gloves, Hestra Job Titan Flex Gloves bring the outstanding comfort and durability of goatskin leather with waterproof neoprene cuffs and Hestra Flex fabric. The stress points on the palm and fingers are reinforced with double-layered leather, while the index fingers and thumbs feature touch-screen pads for convenience. These three-season work gloves are lined with moisture-wicking fleece for added warmth and comfort in cold, wet weather.

In our tests, these gloves provided good waterproof protection and excellent wet-gripping ability. They resisted water penetration for over a minute before moisture found its entry point at the edges of the touch-screen pad on the index finger. The touch-screen pad functioned well, and the glove offered good dexterity and comfort overall, but the sizing runs a bit small. The moderate price point and durable construction make them ideal spring, fall, or mild winter weather general-use work gloves.

Get the Hestra Titan waterproof gloves at Amazon.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, users sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.
